look_here_first: COMPOSITE DROPSEED (*Sporobolus compositus* sensu lato): follow the persistent perennial clump, then a narrowly contracted sometimes partially upper-sheath-enclosed terminal PANICLE of many AWNLESS one-flowered spikelets. The new Bob Harms photographic lessons come from TWO clearly labelled forms: *S. compositus var. drummondii* (SPCOD3-b/i/J0/J1/v; the v side-by-side RIGHT is actually *S. clandestinus*) and *S. compositus var. macer* (SPCOM-b/j1/8). SPCOD3-J0 shows original purple exserted flowering organs, J1 true spikelet-bearing close axis, i open/closed panicle contrast, while SPCOM-8 shows REAL attached scale-covered underground RHIZOME of var. macer ONLY. These features do NOT settle all varieties or *S. clandestinus* separation. Verify an actual rooted specimen and measured intact glumes, smooth lemma surface, and mature pericarp response before species-level final certification.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Latest B043 deep review supports Hays at accepted species rank through var. drummondii, Bexar ecological-site documentation, and Kerr field-succession evidence.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Install and label at species rank. Strict var. compositus Travis material remains disputed and is not used for the PASS decision.

best_field_traits: perennial bunchgrass, substantially taller and more robust than annual poverty dropseed
panicle long and narrow, varying from contracted to somewhat open
spikelets small and numerous along slender panicle branches
persistent perennial crown separates it quickly from annual Sporobolus vaginiflorus
crew_field_check: Perennial bunchgrass with narrow crowded panicles. Distinguish from S. clandestinus by measured glumes/lemmas and fresh mature seed pericarp typically becoming gelatinous and slipping off the seed after wetting; a narrow head alone cannot separate the two. Against S. vaginiflorus, rooted duration and spikelet studies matter.
1-flowered, awnless Sporobolus spikelets — not the multi-flowered bristled clusters of Setaria/Cenchrus.
Photographs of head outline are first clues, NOT confirmed lemma/pericarp identification.
Anther/flower color, panicle width and small/large height alone are not safe identifications.
diagnostic_photo_second_pass_20261022: 1. ROOT/CROWN: use original Cody Stricker green head and genuine Harms drummondii b multi-culm sections to recognize growth architecture; do not call an unrooted panicle a true whole plant.

2. COMPARE varieties honestly: photographer source labels SPCOD3 series *S. compositus var. drummondii* (hairy dropseed) while SPCOM plates are *var. macer* (Mississippi dropseed); these are within a broader species concept but are not blindly interchanged as specimen vouchers.

3. PANICLE: SPCOD3-i shows two measured axis views, one somewhat branching, one tightly enclosed; many tiny awnless spikelets. Source compositus differs from much shorter rough-dropseed genus-matched spikes only with additional organs.

4. ACTUAL FLOWER: SPCOD3-J0 original closeup shows narrow floral-bract units and red-purple exserted reproductive structures at genuine scale. Without pixel-precise floral dissection don't label each tiny curved organ as stigma or anther.

5. ONE SPIKELET: SPCOD3-J1 shows 1-flowered overlapping awnless long narrow spikelets on short branches, with source right-hand scale. Separately measure LOWER glume, UPPER glume and the single floret lemma/palea.

6. AUTHOR'S SIDE BY SIDE: SPCOD3-v has actual author-identified drummondii on LEFT/MIDDLE and **S. clandestinus** on RIGHT. Do not claim all three panels are composite dropseed or that the same-size bar proves both in one fresh local population.

7. SUBTYPE DIFFERENCE: SPCOM-j1 shows var. macer crowded purple drying inflorescence, with many spear-pointed spikelets; similar-looking composite seedheads cannot prove which variety without specimen context.

8. ACTUAL RHIZOME: SPCOM-8 documents horizontal true rootstock with connected ascending bases and roots for **var. macer**. Other varieties usually form tufts and may not have this distinctive rhizome, so don't generalize all *S. compositus* to rhizomatous perennials.

9. WET GRAIN TEST: photograph SAME mature seed before water, during standard timed soaking and after drying; the wet gelatinous pericarp reaction is useful as key evidence, but none of these images proves it. Compare independently determined rough dropseed plus Iowa/FNA sources.

10. FINE FINISH: mature ripe intact spikelet with a 1mm ruler, physically separated glumes and lemma/palea, actual fine hair FRINGE ligule 0.1–0.5mm under macro, 400× exact lemma-surface/hook texture, precise Hays voucher and mobile arrow pixel QA. Otherwise `FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS`.

variety_photo_cautions_20261022.source: Bob Harms Selected Central Texas Monocots
variety_photo_cautions_20261022.potential_variation: Rhizomes seen in var macer only; don't broadly teach composite dropseed as rhizomatous or certify variety from head silhouette
variety_photo_cautions_20261022.comparison_source: SPCOD3-v includes true separately identified S. clandestinus image. These variety names may be treated differently in other taxonomic sources, preserve current canonical treatment.

lookalikes.difference: Also perennial, but rough dropseed is typically recognized by its narrower contracted panicle and rough-textured spikelets; check spikelet pubescence and texture rather than relying on height alone.
Poverty dropseed is an annual, generally smaller, and produces cleistogamous flowers hidden in the upper leaf sheaths.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Check fully mature caryopsis and lemma; preserve whole-plant crown evidence.
field_matrix.difference: Both perennial and similarly headed. Composite dropseed tends to have gelatinizing, separating seed pericarp on fresh wet grains versus persistent/non-gelatinizing in S. clandestinus.
field_matrix.guardrail: The species-complex and varieties have documented identification disagreements; avoid mapping a cultivar/variety from a silhouette.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Compare rooted duration and terminal/axillary panicles.
field_matrix.difference: Annual poverty dropseed frequently has concealed upper-sheath flowering; composite is a perennial and may ALSO form axillary enclosed spikelets.
field_matrix.guardrail: Hidden sheath flowering is not exclusively S. vaginiflorus.

not_reliable_alone: Presence of hidden sheath flowers (multiple related dropseeds can have these)
Being taller/shorter or open/contracted at a single drought-stressed moment
Claiming a micro-lemma character from an ordinary phone photograph

lesson_steps: 1. ROOT/CROWN: use original Cody Stricker green head and genuine Harms drummondii b multi-culm sections to recognize growth architecture; do not call an unrooted panicle a true whole plant.

2. COMPARE varieties honestly: photographer source labels SPCOD3 series *S. compositus var. drummondii* (hairy dropseed) while SPCOM plates are *var. macer* (Mississippi dropseed); these are within a broader species concept but are not blindly interchanged as specimen vouchers.

3. PANICLE: SPCOD3-i shows two measured axis views, one somewhat branching, one tightly enclosed; many tiny awnless spikelets. Source compositus differs from much shorter rough-dropseed genus-matched spikes only with additional organs.

4. ACTUAL FLOWER: SPCOD3-J0 original closeup shows narrow floral-bract units and red-purple exserted reproductive structures at genuine scale. Without pixel-precise floral dissection don't label each tiny curved organ as stigma or anther.

5. ONE SPIKELET: SPCOD3-J1 shows 1-flowered overlapping awnless long narrow spikelets on short branches, with source right-hand scale. Separately measure LOWER glume, UPPER glume and the single floret lemma/palea.

6. AUTHOR'S SIDE BY SIDE: SPCOD3-v has actual author-identified drummondii on LEFT/MIDDLE and **S. clandestinus** on RIGHT. Do not claim all three panels are composite dropseed or that the same-size bar proves both in one fresh local population.

7. SUBTYPE DIFFERENCE: SPCOM-j1 shows var. macer crowded purple drying inflorescence, with many spear-pointed spikelets; similar-looking composite seedheads cannot prove which variety without specimen context.

8. ACTUAL RHIZOME: SPCOM-8 documents horizontal true rootstock with connected ascending bases and roots for **var. macer**. Other varieties usually form tufts and may not have this distinctive rhizome, so don't generalize all *S. compositus* to rhizomatous perennials.

9. WET GRAIN TEST: photograph SAME mature seed before water, during standard timed soaking and after drying; the wet gelatinous pericarp reaction is useful as key evidence, but none of these images proves it. Compare independently determined rough dropseed plus Iowa/FNA sources.

10. FINE FINISH: mature ripe intact spikelet with a 1mm ruler, physically separated glumes and lemma/palea, actual fine hair FRINGE ligule 0.1–0.5mm under macro, 400× exact lemma-surface/hook texture, precise Hays voucher and mobile arrow pixel QA. Otherwise `FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS`.

visual_comparison.title: Composite dropseed — source-verified hairy/macer variety forms, actual flowering units and underground stems
visual_comparison.subtitle: Eight real publicly credited Bob Harms photo references for precisely named S. compositus var. drummondii and var. macer, plus two original in-repo species-level source photos and two different-species comparisons. Source labels preserved, no unsourced broad species claim.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: COMPOSITE DROPSEED COMPLEX: persistent PERENNIAL crown, narrow partly SHEATHED PANICLE of awnless ONE-FLORET spikelets. Bob Harms labels var. drummondii and var. macer separately; macer has pictured RHIZOMES but 'all composite dropseed is rhizomatous' is FALSE. Real lemma and pericarp micro separates from S. clandestinus, not head posture.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Composite dropseed — original flowering variety comparisons, actual spikelet axis and macer rhizome
steps: 1. ROOT/CROWN: use original Cody Stricker green head and genuine Harms drummondii b multi-culm sections to recognize growth architecture; do not call an unrooted panicle a true whole plant.

2. COMPARE varieties honestly: photographer source labels SPCOD3 series *S. compositus var. drummondii* (hairy dropseed) while SPCOM plates are *var. macer* (Mississippi dropseed); these are within a broader species concept but are not blindly interchanged as specimen vouchers.

3. PANICLE: SPCOD3-i shows two measured axis views, one somewhat branching, one tightly enclosed; many tiny awnless spikelets. Source compositus differs from much shorter rough-dropseed genus-matched spikes only with additional organs.

4. ACTUAL FLOWER: SPCOD3-J0 original closeup shows narrow floral-bract units and red-purple exserted reproductive structures at genuine scale. Without pixel-precise floral dissection don't label each tiny curved organ as stigma or anther.

5. ONE SPIKELET: SPCOD3-J1 shows 1-flowered overlapping awnless long narrow spikelets on short branches, with source right-hand scale. Separately measure LOWER glume, UPPER glume and the single floret lemma/palea.

6. AUTHOR'S SIDE BY SIDE: SPCOD3-v has actual author-identified drummondii on LEFT/MIDDLE and **S. clandestinus** on RIGHT. Do not claim all three panels are composite dropseed or that the same-size bar proves both in one fresh local population.

7. SUBTYPE DIFFERENCE: SPCOM-j1 shows var. macer crowded purple drying inflorescence, with many spear-pointed spikelets; similar-looking composite seedheads cannot prove which variety without specimen context.

8. ACTUAL RHIZOME: SPCOM-8 documents horizontal true rootstock with connected ascending bases and roots for **var. macer**. Other varieties usually form tufts and may not have this distinctive rhizome, so don't generalize all *S. compositus* to rhizomatous perennials.

9. WET GRAIN TEST: photograph SAME mature seed before water, during standard timed soaking and after drying; the wet gelatinous pericarp reaction is useful as key evidence, but none of these images proves it. Compare independently determined rough dropseed plus Iowa/FNA sources.

10. FINE FINISH: mature ripe intact spikelet with a 1mm ruler, physically separated glumes and lemma/palea, actual fine hair FRINGE ligule 0.1–0.5mm under macro, 400× exact lemma-surface/hook texture, precise Hays voucher and mobile arrow pixel QA. Otherwise `FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS`.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Use visible macro morphology first and defer difficult perennial-species separations to mature material, reliable grain tests and microscope when necessary.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Bob Harms source photographs show *S. compositus var. drummondii* OR *var. macer*, which may be treated differently in floras. The source comparison v includes the different species *S. clandestinus*. Do not interpret macer rhizome as universal or pretend a wet grain pericarp experiment was photographed.

True ~0.1–0.5mm ciliate ligule hair fringe photographed at actual upper blade/sheath junction under 20–40x source-valid microscope, with 0.5mm reference and no invented arrow.

Fresh ripe grain filmed before and after water with a precisely documented interval and 1mm ruler, with visible pericarp swelling/slipping and same-plant ID (key varies with specimens and seasonal grain maturity).

Vouchered comparison *Sporobolus compositus* varietal units and *S. clandestinus* intact mature glumes/lemmas and grain with true same-scale microscope; Harms photo v is a useful source-labelled side-by-side but not clean standalone species proof.
Review any microscopic true lemma surface hooks/silica cells at ≥400× and check the 4 existing annotation arrows on the mobile public website after publication.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: A persistent tuft and crowded, narrow panicle
field_id_short_tiles.details: Look for a perennial clump with a contracted terminal or upper-sheath-enclosed panicle. Iowa's grass treatment describes flowering heads about 5–26 cm long and 0.5–1.5 cm wide with branches appressed to the axis. The existing Harms SPCOD3 and SPCOM photographs represent TWO source-labelled varieties; they are not interchangeable Hays vouchers. Head outline cannot separate rough dropseed.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PANICLE PHOTO PRESENT; LOCAL ROOTED VOUCHER MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · GROWTH FORM AND LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.details: Culms commonly 45–130 cm in the Iowa treatment, with a true ligule of fine hairs approximately 0.1–0.5 mm at the inner blade/sheath junction. Variety macer has documented creeping scaly RHIZOMES in Harms SPCOM-8; do NOT teach rhizomes as universal for the whole species. Existing photos do not resolve individual ligule hairs at calibrated magnification.
field_id_short_tiles.status: VAR. MACER RHIZOME VISIBLE; MEASURED LIGULE MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE ONE MATURE SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: One floret; approximately 4.5–5.4 mm in Iowa key
field_id_short_tiles.details: A ripe composite-dropseed spikelet is generally single-flowered, laterally compressed, and AWNLESS. The Iowa treatment reports approximately 4.5–5.4 mm, while broader regional concepts include wider values. The Harms SPCOD3-J1 and SPCOM-j1 show real spikelet units but not a detached, independently measured complete glume/lemma/palea series.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES AND LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two shorter glumes, smooth one-veined lemma
field_id_short_tiles.details: Iowa grass treatment: lower glume approximately 2.6–3.5 mm, upper glume 3.2–4.8 mm, both usually one-veined; fertile lemma approximately 4.4–5.2 mm, smooth, one-veined and awnless; palea 3.9–4.9 mm, two-veined. These are published measurements, NOT measurements of the existing photographs. Photograph separate mature bracts with a 1-mm scale before placing organ-specific arrows.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · SEED TEST IS A HOLD
field_id_short_tiles.short: Conflicting wet-pericarp literature: do not teach a binary test
field_id_short_tiles.details: Some Harms/USFS accounts describe a mature composite-dropseed pericarp that gelatinizes or slips on wetting, whereas a Go Botany key assigns conflicting wet-pericarp states. Preserve this source disagreement and species/variety concepts. Do NOT identify a field plant by an unverified water-drop test or label any existing dry seed photo as gelatinized. Require independent voucher, timed fresh-seed series and source reconciliation.
field_id_short_tiles.status: CONFLICT HELD; NO CERTIFIED WET TEST

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · SEPARATE THE THREE DROPSEEDS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Perennial rough dropseed and annual poverty dropseed
field_id_short_tiles.details: S. clandestinus is another perennial with a tightly contracted panicle; it requires mature glume/lemma and specialist lemma-surface/pericarp work for reliable separation. S. vaginiflorus is generally an annual with terminal and upper-sheath flowering; other dropseeds may also hide flowers. The Harms SPCOD3-v right panel is S. clandestinus, NOT composite dropseed. Record Sporobolus sp. if no mature diagnostic evidence.
field_id_short_tiles.status: COMPARISONS DOCUMENTED; MATCHED REPRODUCTIVE MACROS MISSING
